prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: From, When, Stop

outputs.L1:
From the old bridge where we had been stopped,  
a little below us, it looked like a diving board.  
When the girl switched her sign from **Stop** to **Slow**,  
I saw, across the river, three men standing like old-fashioned divers  
at its base—newsreels we had seen of men in swim caps.  
“Hard hats,” you said, literal as ever.

You agreed with “like a diving board,”  
but noted there was no spring to it. Something below  
was holding it up, something concrete.  
It was the business of your life. Concrete—  
but for me, the men were waiting their turn over there,  
each to compete for the best two-and-a-half gainer  
to knife the Tye River.

“They’d die,” you said.

“That’s a fine span,” I learned,  
“a very long one—they didn’t make ’em like that back then.”  
Or us either, I thought,  
as I almost saw the hard hat bounce at the tip,  
one knee lifted to his waist.

“Inspectors,” you said as we drove across,  
“lollygagging.”

Whichever. Our span is ready.
outputs.L2:
From the aging bridge where traffic had held us up,  
the structure just below seemed, from where we sat,  
almost like a diving platform.  

When the flagger changed her paddle  
from **Stop** to **Slow**,  
I noticed, on the far side of the river,  
three men gathered at the end of it,  
posed like divers from some old newsreel—  
the kind we had watched, with men in bathing caps.  

“Hard hats,” you corrected me,  
always so exact.  

You accepted the “diving board” comparison,  
though you pointed out it had no bounce.  
Something underneath supported it—  
some solid thing, something made of concrete.  
That was the work you knew,  
the material of your life.  

Concrete, yes. But to me,  
those men still looked as if they were lined up,  
each waiting for his turn,  
each about to attempt the finest  
two-and-a-half gainer  
and slice into the Tye River below.  

They’d be killed, you said.  

“That’s an impressive span,” I came to understand,  
“a very long one—  
they didn’t build them that way in those days.”  
Nor did they build us that way, I thought,  
as I almost imagined the man in the hard hat  
springing from the end,  
one knee lifted high to his waist.  

“Inspectors,” you said while we crossed over,  
“standing around wasting time.”  

Maybe so.  
In any case, our own crossing is ready.
outputs.L3:
From a distance, the speaker looks at a bridge and allows the scene to become something more than an ordinary piece of infrastructure. Rather than seeing only a structure made of concrete and designed for crossing, the speaker imagines the bridge as a kind of diving board, suspended above the space below it. This imaginative comparison transforms the bridge from a practical object into a stage for possibility, risk, and performance.

Near the bridge, the speaker notices three men wearing hard hats. In a literal sense, they may be workers, inspectors, or engineers examining the structure. Yet the speaker’s imagination reshapes them into figures from another world: old-fashioned divers preparing to leap. Their hard hats become part of a costume, and their work near the bridge is reimagined as a theatrical act. Through this vision, the ordinary becomes playful and strange.

The speaker’s companion, however, responds to the scene in a more practical way. Instead of entering into the speaker’s fantasy, the companion sees the bridge for what it physically is: a concrete span, an engineered structure with real weight, function, and design. This literal interpretation emphasizes construction, stability, and purpose. For the companion, the bridge is not a diving board but an object to be understood through its materials and engineering.

This contrast between the two perspectives is central to the poem. The speaker approaches the world through imagination, metaphor, and transformation, while the companion focuses on factual observation and practical reality. The bridge inspectors become, in the speaker’s mind, performers poised for a dive. What one person sees as maintenance or engineering, the other sees as drama and spectacle.

At the same time, the bridge itself becomes symbolic. Its physical span suggests connection, not only between two sides of a landscape but also between the speaker and the companion. Their different ways of seeing create distance between them, yet the shared act of looking at the bridge also links them. The poem uses the bridge to explore how relationships depend on both separation and connection, practicality and imagination, literal sight and visionary interpretation.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a quiet but meaningful contrast between two people looking at the same scene in very different ways. On the surface, the subject is a bridge inspection, but the speaker immediately transforms the event into something more imaginative and symbolic. Instead of seeing only workers examining a structure, the speaker pictures them almost like divers, moving through an underwater world. This metaphor gives the bridge a sense of mystery and depth, as if the inspection is not merely technical but also emotional and exploratory.

The speaker’s companion, however, responds in a much more practical way. Rather than entering into the speaker’s imaginative vision, the companion focuses on the engineering purpose of the inspection: the bridge must be tested, measured, and confirmed as safe. This difference reveals a deeper tension between the two figures. One sees metaphor, beauty, and hidden meaning; the other sees function, structure, and responsibility. Their separate interpretations of the bridge suggest separate ways of understanding life itself.

The word “span” becomes especially important because it refers not only to the physical reach of the bridge from one side to the other, but also to the emotional distance between the speaker and the companion. A bridge is meant to connect, yet in the poem it also reveals separation. The inspection may show that the bridge is structurally sound and ready to carry weight, but the relationship between the two people seems less certain. Their bond may exist, but their different perspectives suggest a gap that is difficult to cross.

In this way, the bridge becomes a central metaphor for the relationship. It represents connection, support, and the possibility of crossing from one side to another. At the same time, it emphasizes distance and difference. The poem suggests that relationships, like bridges, must be examined carefully: they may appear strong, but their true condition depends on what lies beneath the surface. By contrasting imagination with practicality, the poem shows how two people can share the same moment while experiencing it in entirely different ways.
outputs.L5:
**From When to Stop**

From the moment we begin something new, we often focus on how to move forward. We ask ourselves when the right time is to start, when we will see results, and when success will finally arrive. But just as important as knowing when to begin is knowing when to stop.

Stopping does not always mean failure. Sometimes, it means wisdom. We may need to stop a habit that holds us back, stop worrying about things we cannot control, or stop waiting for the “perfect” moment. From every experience, we learn that timing matters. When we listen to ourselves and understand our limits, we become stronger and more aware.

Life is full of movement, choices, and changes. Knowing when to continue and when to stop helps us grow in the right direction.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free-verse poem about being stopped on an old bridge during roadwork, seeing hard-hatted inspectors on a structure over the Tye River, and turning it into a metaphor for a relationship.
counterfactuals.output:
At the temporary light  
on the old bridge over the Tye,  
I put the car in park  
and let the engine idle down  
to its small, worried prayer.

Ahead, men in hard hats  
walk the ribs of the structure,  
touching beams, pointing,  
nodding at places where rust  
has bloomed under paint.

One kneels to look  
beneath the rail.  
Another writes something  
on a clipboard  
as if the bridge has confessed.

The river keeps moving below them,  
brown-green, indifferent,  
carrying leaves, rainwater,  
whatever the mountains have let go.

I think of us then—  
how long we kept crossing  
without looking underneath.

How we trusted the span  
because it had held before,  
because it had a name,  
because everyone else  
seemed to get across.

But love, too, has joints  
weather loosens.  
Bolts that remember  
every winter.  
Weight limits  
no one wants to read aloud.

Maybe this is mercy:  
the flagger’s palm raised,  
the forced pause,  
the orange cones saying  
not yet, not like this.

Maybe repair begins  
with standing still  
in the lane we thought  
would always be open,

watching strangers  
measure the damage  
with practiced hands,

while below us  
the Tye River goes on  
making its argument  
for passage,

for patience,

for the long work  
of holding.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary poem in the voice of someone riding with a practical partner across an old bridge, where a construction scene resembles divers on a diving board and the speaker reflects on “our span.”
counterfactuals.output:
We cross the old bridge in your dented car,  
you naming the useful things—  
load limit, weathering, the cost of steel,  
how rivets loosen in a winter like this.  

Below us, the river lifts its dull green back.  
Beside the far pier, men in hard hats  
stand along a plank of scaffolding,  
one after another, poised above the air—  
not workers now, but divers  
on a diving board, waiting  
for the whistle of some bright summer pool.  

You say, They’ll close a lane by Friday.  
I say nothing, watching them balance  
between repair and plunge,  
their orange vests small flames  
against the gray, their hands  
full of tools and weather.  

This is how you love the world:  
by asking what holds,  
what must be mended,  
what fails if left alone.  

And I, less practical, keep seeing  
water everywhere—under us, over us,  
time running its cold fingers  
through the trusses.  

Still, we ride on together,  
your eyes measuring distance,  
mine measuring light,  
the bridge groaning softly  
as if remembering every crossing.  

I think of our span—  
not endless, no,  
but made of tension,  
of weight accepted,  
of two shores needing each other  
and the trembling structure between.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a narrative poem with dialogue, using the phrases “Stop to Slow,” “like a diving board,” “Hard hats,” “That’s a fine span,” and ending with “Our span is ready.”
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn beside the river’s silver bend,  
the foreman raised his hand and called, “Attend—  
today we lift the beams, today we throw  
our courage where the quick dark waters flow.”

A sign swung near the gravel road below:  
“Stop to Slow,” it warned the trucks in line,  
while morning warmed the cranes to gold and pine.

“Hard hats,” cried Mae, “and steady hands, my friends.  
A bridge begins where one shore ends.”  
Old Joseph laughed, his toolbox scarred and broad:  
“That’s a fine span for folks to cross, by God.”

The first beam rose, like a diving board  
over the current’s restless roar.  
A boy watched wide-eyed from the clay:  
“Will it hold the whole town one day?”

Mae smiled. “If we build it true and tight,  
it will hold the dusk, the dawn, the night.  
It will hold your footsteps, rain and snow,  
and all the places you will go.”

By noon the cables sang in sun,  
by dusk the final bolts were done.  
The river hushed beneath the light,  
two banks clasped hands across the night.

Old Joseph touched the rail with pride:  
“Tomorrow, we walk to the other side.”  
Mae looked out where the waters ran,  
and softly said to every woman, child, and man:

“Our span is ready.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem in the style of a mid-century American confessional/observational poet, blending road construction, bridge inspection, the Tye River, and quiet tension between “you” and “I.”
counterfactuals.output:
At the temporary light  
where the road narrows to one lane,  
we sit in the idling car  
with the windows cracked,  
the flagman’s vest burning orange  
against the wet shale bank.

All morning the machines have worried the mountain—  
backhoes clawing at the shoulder,  
dump trucks backing up with their small,  
insistent grief.  
A sign says  
BRIDGE INSPECTION AHEAD  
as if a bridge were a body  
and someone, finally,  
had been called to touch each joint,  
tap each rusted place,  
write down what might fail.

Below us the Tye River  
moves as it always has,  
brown-green, muscular,  
carrying leaves, foam,  
the pale undersides of sycamores  
broken into light.

You say nothing.  
I say nothing better.

Men in hard hats lean over the rail  
with clipboards and hammers,  
listening for hollowness  
in the steel.  
One kneels to photograph  
a crack no wider than a hair.  
Another points beneath the deck  
where water has been making its argument  
for years.

I think of all the things  
we have crossed without looking down.

The stopped cars accumulate behind us,  
a patient line of strangers  
keeping their engines alive.  
Somewhere a radio mutters weather.  
Somewhere gravel drops  
from a raised bed  
like a sentence unfinished.

You keep your hands  
folded in your lap.  
I watch the river  
touch each pier and divide,  
then find itself again  
on the other side.

When the light changes,  
no one moves at first.  
Even the flagman hesitates,  
his sign turned slow  
from STOP to SLOW,  
as if he understands  
there are distances  
a road cannot measure,

and bridges that remain standing  
only because we do not ask them  
what they have endured.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem about an old bridge that looks like a diving board, with three men in hard hats at its base, a literal-minded companion, and an implied meditation on marriage or partnership.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Old Bridge**

The old bridge juts from the cliffside  
like a diving board no one dares use,  
its planks silvered by weather,  
its railings gone to rust and rumor.

At its base, three men in hard hats  
stand around a hole in the road,  
pointing with the solemnity  
of priests at an uncooperative god.

You say, “It looks like it wants to leap.”

My companion frowns.  
“Bridges don’t want things.  
And that isn’t water down there—  
it’s drainage, gravel, probably rebar.”

The wind moves through the cables  
with its old married sound:  
not music exactly,  
not complaint.

We stand a while, not speaking,  
above the distance we have agreed  
not to measure too often.

Below us, the men keep working—  
one holding the plans,  
one holding the shovel,  
one simply watching the others,  
as if every crossing needs witnesses.

“Anyway,” my companion says,  
“a diving board ends where it ends.”

But this bridge, stubborn with age,  
keeps reaching from one side  
toward another,  
held up by bolts, habit,  
and a faith too plain to name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
